title: How Albany educrats turned NY’s once-proud schools into a national joke tional-joke/
author: Robert Pondiscio
summary: Robert Pondiscio, a former South Bronx fifth-grade teacher, responds to the New York Board of Regents' decision to end the requirement that students pass Regents exams to graduate, starting with the class of 2028. He recalls panelists on an Albany NPR show laughing when he cited Mississippi as a literacy model, even though Mississippi's fourth graders, including Black and Hispanic students, now outperform New York's in reading at a fraction of the cost. Pondiscio contrasts today's Albany with the Bloomberg-Klein era, when reformers believed poor children could achieve at high levels and treated failure as a call for better teaching. He lists the steps by which the state weakened expectations, from expanded appeals and credit recovery to ending teacher literacy tests and capping charters. His conclusion is that New York's educational pride has outlived the ambition that once justified it.
points: Mississippi's fourth graders outperformed New York's in reading on the latest NAEP.
By 2018 nearly half of New York City high schools used credit recovery programs.
New York eliminated a basic literacy skills test for prospective teachers in 2017.
A Regent defended the change by saying you do not assess a fish on climbing a tree, which Pondiscio rejects.
He argues reading, writing, and math are not innate talents but what schools exist to instill.
quotes: When I mentioned that Mississippi has become a national model for improving children’s literacy, my fellow panelists laughed out loud.
Underlying it was a bedrock belief that poor children can achieve at high levels.
Worse, Albany has spent much of the past two decades weakening expectations and abandoning accountability mechanisms designed to produce better results.
Reading, writing, mathematics, science and history aren’t innate talents that some children possess and others simply don’t.
There’s nothing compassionate about looking at a child who has not been taught well and concluding that perhaps reading proficiency was the wrong thing to demand of him.
And when children failed to meet an academic standard, their first impulse was to ask what adults must do differently.
The embarrassing thing isn’t that New York might have something to learn from Mississippi: It’s that we still find the idea funny.
